source.title: Nexusformer: Nonlinear Attention Expansion for Stable and Inheritable Transformer Scaling
source.authors: Wei-Jie Zhao; Mingquan Liu; Bo-Lun Wang; Simon Wu; Nuobei Xie; Rui Zhu; Peng-Yang Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations, tables, and figure text are flattened or garbled, but the document is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It reports language-model perplexity and downstream performance across model sizes and continued-training budgets, bearing on scale-related loss and performance trends, but uses its own architecture and experimental setup rather than reproducing the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier scaling laws and discusses data-limited regimes, but cited findings are not recorded as rows. Main-scale Table 1 reports downstream scores, not held-out loss. Table 2's aggregate downstream scores and Table 8's PPL results are recorded. Table 4 reports loss across continued-training snapshots and initialization conditions. The paper's geometric-radius-to-PPL fit is recorded as a finding outside the listed versions because its predictor is not parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. Its results compare its own method (Nexusformer) with baselines (TokenFormer, Qwen3, Transformer++) at matched sizes. It fits no power law of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. The size ranges are 240M–440M for perplexity (under 2x) and 170M–640M for downstream scores, and runs differ in training path (progressive growth vs from scratch), so no row bears on V1–V7. Kaplan-style scaling laws appear only as framing and as a post-hoc explanation for an observed loss rebound (App. I). The paper's own 'scaling law' predicts PPL from a geometric radius R, not from N, D or C.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Nexusformer's nonlinear Q/K/V projections enable lossless, inheritable growth and outperform baselines from 170M to 640M. It matches Tokenformer's perplexity with up to 41.5% less compute in 240M→440M progressive scaling. Zero initialization gives a stable diverge-then-converge trajectory, and a geometric-radius 'scaling law' predicts PPL. They attribute the loss rebound and score plateau to a data-limited regime, citing Kaplan's L(N,D) without fitting it. They concede the 640M/100B-token scale is modest and the R fit uses only three settings.
record.recipe_differences: New nonlinear attention architecture and progressive model expansion; experiments use a limited 240M–440M growth range and also compare models trained at several sizes. This is not the original parameter/token/compute scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies initialization perturbation (zero, Noise 10%, Noise 20%) and continued-training token count. It also discusses fixed data and fixed learning-rate choices as relevant to scaling behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: ln(PPL) = −0.0991·|ln(R)| + 2.4804 (R²=0.658) across three expansion settings, where R is a geometric alignment radius.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Nexusformer growth, a parameter-distribution alignment radius R predicts PPL.

fits_no_version.finding: After zero-init expansion (240M→380M), loss rises to 2.6416 at 15B tokens, then falls to 2.3337 at 30B. The 10% and 20% noise inits give nearly identical losses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-expansion continued-training loss follows a diverge-then-converge trajectory; initialization noise barely changes the loss.

record.problems: The largest tested model is 640M, which the authors describe as modest relative to contemporary models. They state their geometric scaling-law fit is based on only three expansion settings. The paper does not report a conventional power-law fit of held-out loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute. Some training-loss values are not explicitly identified as held-out loss, and the downstream aggregates are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within 60 rows, Table 1 aggregate rows for TokenFormer at 170M, 240M, and 640M were omitted; Table 1 aggregate rows for Transformer++ at all four sizes were omitted; and individual downstream benchmark scores were omitted in favor of the table's reported five-benchmark average. Table 2 individual benchmark scores were likewise omitted in favor of its reported average. Table 8 PPL rows for these same sizes were retained.

untested.parts: No loss-vs-N/D/C power-law fit; ranges under one order of magnitude.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No controlled depth/width sweep at fixed parameter count.
Text only; no other modality or regime fits.
No fit of downstream score on scale or loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader over-linked rows to V1, V4, V6 and V7 and issued verdicts from a method-comparison study. All verdicts should be dropped. Qwen3 trained from scratch shows monotonic PPL decline over 240–440M (18.17→12.25), but per-model token counts are unclear and the span is under 2x, so it is not usable for V1. App. I's claim that 'all models exhibit a rebound in validation loss' is not supported by any reported curve: the Table 8 PPLs for Qwen3 decrease monotonically.

versions.untested_parts: It does not establish power-law fits against parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude, nor isolate regimes where the other factors are not bottlenecks.
No fit on small runs is used to predict the losses of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of the parameter/token allocation or fit of their growth with compute is reported.
The comparisons are between distinct model architectures at matched parameter counts; they do not isolate depth, width, or other individual architecture changes.
Only language-model training is reported; other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The study reports benchmark scores across sizes but does not fit or test a predictor from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
The paper reports a loss rebound and a limited-scale fit, but does not compare fitted exponents across alternative fitting choices or establish disagreement between published laws.

rows.operation_detail: Compared PPL across model sizes and architectures
rows.measure: PPL
rows.note: At matched size, Qwen3's reported PPL is 18.1741; the study does not isolate architecture details.
rows.check: Table 8 compares the study's method with Qwen3 at matched sizes, which is method-vs-baseline, not a scaling test. V4 concerns depth or width within an architecture; a different attention projection is not a shape change. Nexusformer sizes 300–440M are progressive-growth checkpoints with different training paths. The span is under 2x, so it cannot show a power law or a bend.
